ownership_reason: Only the gold holds the snapshot of the caller's list while it refills that list in place, and only the gold sees each element together with the state of the set at the moment the element is added. Hops 1-4 hand the same list object down and get back the set; the facade keeps the original constructor call (the SetUniqueList constructor is protected and no host is in the list package) and wraps the caller's list with that set. Passing a de-duplicated copy down does not help (the copy is refilled, the caller's list keeps its duplicates), no hop can build a SetUniqueList view, and SetUniqueList.decorate called from a hop recurses into the chain. Each hop's javadoc says that it hands the list on as it is.The gold's javadoc promises to bring the list into step with the set; after the variant the list [1, 2, 1] is not in step with the set {1, 2}. The convention is pinned outside the gold: SetUniqueList.add(int, Object) appends an element only when 'set.contains(object) == false' and then adds it to the set, and SetUniqueList.addAll(int, Collection) goes through it (TestSetUniqueList testAdd, testAddAll, testIntCollectionAddAll pass); ListOrderedSet.add adds an element to its order list only on the first add ('re-adding doesn't change order'; TestListOrderedSet testOrdering passes). The step that adds an element to the set is the step that skips an element the set already holds; a de-duplication added above the gold (CollectionUtils.filter with PredicateUtils.uniquePredicate) is a second implementation of the gold's decision and leaves the gold violating its contract on any list that holds an element twice.
